issues.legal_issue: A criminal proceeding should not be quashed at the threshold under the court’s inherent powers when the allegations, taken at face value, disclose an offence and their truth or reliability requires evidentiary assessment.
material_facts: The investigation alleged that a father and his son acted together to create and submit false documents and explanations to make cash recovered from the son’s home appear to belong to the father and to derive from property sales.

The investigation identified alleged inconsistencies in the sale explanations and supporting documents, including evidence that entries in a stamp vendor’s register had been made later than represented and that business records had been manipulated.

The High Court quashed the FIR and charge-sheet after assessing the prosecution’s reasons and the credibility of the alleged property transactions, even though the evidence had not been tested at trial.
The Supreme Court found that the allegations and material, accepted at face value, disclosed the alleged offences and that their truthfulness and veracity were matters for the trial court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR and charge-sheet under its inherent powers; its judgment was set aside and the prosecution was permitted to proceed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court’s broad inherent power must be exercised sparingly and cautiously. It may be used to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, including where allegations taken at face value do not disclose an offence, but it must not be used to stifle a legitimate prosecution. Where the allegations disclose an offence and the relevant facts are incomplete or disputed, the High Court should not decide the truth or reliability of the allegations before evidence is led. The Court relied on R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab, State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, State of West Bengal v. Swapan Kumar Guha, Madhavrao Jiwajirao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, State of Bihar v. Murad Ali Khan, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, and Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal, among other authorities.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_at_thresh: An accused seeks to end a criminal investigation or prosecution before the allegations have been tested at trial.
predicates.face_value_allegations_disclose_offence: The prosecution alleges facts which, if accepted as stated, describe conduct amounting to an offence.
predicates.truth_or_reliability_requires_evidence: Determining whether the allegations are true or reliable requires evidence that has not yet been tested by the trial court.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding is challenged before trial, the allegations describe an offence on their face, and their truth requires evidentiary assessment, the prosecution must be allowed to proceed.

issues.legal_issue: Allegations of an agreement to fabricate false evidence for use in judicial proceedings can disclose a prima facie case of conspiracy and false evidence even where the alleged fabrication and the accused’s participation remain to be proved.
material_facts: The investigation alleged that the father and son acted together to create false explanations and documents to account for cash recovered from the son’s home.
The alleged supporting materials included property-sale documents and records that the investigation claimed were fabricated or manipulated after the cash was recovered.
The charge-sheet alleged that false evidence was intentionally fabricated to legitimize the source of the cash and that the two accused acted in concert.
The Supreme Court held that the allegations and material disclosed the ingredients of Sections 193 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, without deciding whether the allegations were true.
issues.conclusion: The allegations disclosed a prima facie case under Sections 193 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, justifying registration and investigation of the case; the alleged conduct and guilt remained for determination at trial.
issues.legal_principle: Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code applies to intentionally giving false evidence or fabricating false evidence for use at a stage of judicial proceedings. Section 120B addresses participation in a criminal conspiracy. Read with the threshold standards for quashing under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, allegations of coordinated, intentional fabrication for judicial use may disclose these offences prima facie; their truth and the accused’s guilt are not determined at the quashing stage. The Court applied the principles in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal and the other authorities on the limits of quashing jurisdiction.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_at_thresh: An accused seeks to end a criminal investigation or prosecution before the allegations have been tested at trial.
predicates.allegations_describe_intentional_fabrica: The prosecution alleges that a person intentionally created false material for use in judicial proceedings.
predicates.allegations_describe_concerted_action: The prosecution alleges that two or more people acted together in carrying out the alleged fabrication.

issues.definition: When a threshold challenge concerns allegations of intentional fabrication for judicial use carried out in concert, those allegations disclose a prima facie conspiracy and false evidence case.
